name: Oxymetazoline cream (Rhofade)

card.summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor cream approved in 2017 for persistent facial redness of rosacea; it narrows vessels for a temporary reduction in redness.
card.note: Prescription-only in the US; effect lasts only while applied, and the same drug in nasal sprays is known for rebound congestion.

quick.overview:
Rhofade is a 1% oxymetazoline cream that the FDA approved in January 2017 for persistent facial redness (erythema) in adults with rosacea. Oxymetazoline is the same decongestant ingredient found in nasal sprays such as Afrin.

It is discussed in skincare circles as a temporary redness reducer that works by shrinking blood vessels in the skin. It is a prescription product in the US; reviews in prescribing journals evaluated its approval.
quick.mechanism: Oxymetazoline is a direct-acting sympathomimetic that mainly activates alpha-1 and, to a lesser degree, alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, narrowing small blood vessels. In the skin this reduces visible redness while the drug is present.
quick.risks: The nasal-spray form is known for rebound congestion with prolonged use. For the cream, prescribing reviews describe local skin reactions as the main adverse effects; consult the label for full details. It is prescription-only in the US.

lead: Oxymetazoline cream (brand name Rhofade) is a prescription 1% topical formulation of the alpha-adrenergic agonist oxymetazoline, approved by the US FDA in January 2017 for persistent facial erythema associated with rosacea in adults.[1][4] It narrows the small blood vessels of the facial skin, so that skin looks less red and more even in tone for the hours the drug is active, which is why it is discussed by people who want a calmer, less flushed complexion.[8][10]

Oxymetazoline itself is an older drug, developed from xylometazoline at Merck in 1961 and sold as a nasal decongestant (Afrin and others), with eye-drop and eyelid-lift uses as well.[4] The cream was reviewed in American Family Physician, The Medical Letter and drug-approval summaries.[1][2][3] Pivotal phase 3 trials, a 52-week extension and a 2023 meta-analysis of 2,298 participants describe how much redness reduction users can expect and the local reactions that occur.[9][11][12]

Brimonidine gel was previously the only product approved specifically for rosacea redness, and oxymetazoline cream is the second such alpha agonist.[13] Both are treatments of the redness itself rather than of the underlying inflammatory process, and are often combined in practice with other rosacea therapies or with vascular lasers.[14][15]
infobox: Nasal decongestant, eye redness drops, eyelid ptosis solution (Upneeq)[4]

paras: The approved indication is persistent facial redness associated with rosacea in adults [1][4]. Rosacea overviews list oxymetazoline alongside brimonidine as vasoconstrictor topicals, with less detailed evidence for oxymetazoline in that reference [6].

The label indication covers persistent facial redness in adults and does not cover the papules and pustules of rosacea, which are treated with other agents such as metronidazole, azelaic acid, ivermectin or minocycline.[13][14] Rosacea overviews list brimonidine and oxymetazoline together as vasoconstrictor options for the redness component.[6][14] Clinicians have also described its use together with pulsed dye laser: a randomised pilot trial of 34 patients with erythematotelangiectatic rosacea compared three monthly 595-nm laser sessions plus oxymetazoline with oxymetazoline alone and followed 25 completers for six months.[15]

Oxymetazoline is an imidazole-derived direct-acting sympathomimetic that activates alpha-1 and, partially, alpha-2 adrenergic receptors; reviews describe the cream as primarily an alpha-1A agonist whose vasoconstriction of cutaneous vessels diminishes erythema.[4][9][12] Vascular beds widely express alpha-1 receptors, and local alpha-2 activation on vessel endothelium also constricts vessels.[4] Merck developed it from xylometazoline in 1961 and the Afrin nasal spray reached over-the-counter status in 1975.[4] A dedicated pharmacokinetic study of the cream applied to the face in rosacea patients examined systemic exposure after topical administration.[16] After systemic absorption of the drug the elimination half-life is reported as 5 to 8 hours.[4]

A review of the nasal spray found that use beyond about three days can cause rebound congestion.[4] For the facial cream, a 2023 meta-analysis of 2,298 participants reported treatment-related adverse events in about 7 percent, with local reactions including stinging or burning (15 percent), itching (15 percent), dryness (23 percent) and scaling (17 percent), and a rebound rate of erythema of about 1 percent.[11] Safety and tolerability with laser or energy-based therapy was studied in a 46-person phase 4 trial.[7] The product label and the cited reviews give the full profile.[1][3]

Wikipedia lists Rhofade as the cream brand, with other oxymetazoline brands such as Afrin, Visine L.R. and Upneeq for other uses; oxymetazoline ranked about 305th among US prescriptions in 2022.[4] Eyelid droop treatment with the ophthalmic solution was approved by the FDA in July 2020, and a topical form coded DA-020 was reported to be at preclinical stage for hair loss as of March 2026.[4] The Medical Letter's 2024 overview of rosacea drugs places the cream among options for redness.[20]

Phase 2 dose-ranging work in persistent facial erythema of rosacea preceded two identically designed randomised phase 3 trials of once-daily oxymetazoline 1% against vehicle.[17][12] In a pooled analysis of those trials, a clinically relevant reduction in erythema was reported on the first day of treatment.[8] A long-term study reported high and sustained efficacy through 52 weeks of daily use.[9] A later phase 4 analysis of standardised photographs from the phase 3 trials (835 patients, 415 oxymetazoline and 420 vehicle) found significantly more oxymetazoline-treated patients achieved a one-grade Clinician Erythema Assessment improvement at 1 to 12 hours after dosing, and examined how allowing reviewers to refer to baseline photographs changed measured vehicle response.[18]

The 2023 systematic review pooled 2,298 participants and found that at week 4, 38 percent (95% CI 28 to 48) reached a two-grade CEA improvement and 25 percent (22 to 27) a two-grade improvement on the subject self-assessment.[11] A comprehensive review of the evidence and a 2017 pharmacology review describe the same programme.[12][19] Other registered work includes a 1,105-participant clinical-endpoint bioequivalence trial (NCT03954444) and the 46-person phase 4 energy-based therapy study (NCT03380390).[5][7]

The cream is discussed as a short-term option for facial redness, in the same breath as brimonidine gel and in-clinic vascular lasers. Because the effect is described as lasting while the drug is active rather than permanently clearing redness, discussion tends to centre on timing for events and on combining it with laser or other rosacea therapy.[15]

chain: Applied once daily to the central face
Activates alpha-1A receptors and constricts surface vessels
Persistent redness appears reduced while the drug is active
angle.text: Oxymetazoline cream is applied to facial skin to reduce the visible redness of rosacea. In trials the proportion of participants showing a clinician-rated improvement began to separate from vehicle within hours of the first application.
